syntax:
const path = require("path");
console.log(path.join("folder", "file.txt"));
explain: require loads a module. path builds file paths that work on every computer.
example: Finding the data folder next to server.js.

explain: fs reads and writes files. Sync versions wait until the file is done.
example: This app saves your notes to /data this way.

explain: The promise version of fs, used with async and await so other work can go on meanwhile.
example: A server that reads files without blocking other visitors.

explain: JSON.parse turns text into an object. JSON.stringify turns it back into text.
example: Reading and saving a JSON settings file.

explain: process tells you about the running program: the Node version, the command-line words, and environment variables.
example: Reading a secret API key from an environment variable.

explain: Express makes a web server. app.get answers a page request. It needs npm install express, so read it rather than run it here.

syntax:
npm init -y
npm install express
npm start
explain: Terminal commands: create package.json, install a package, run the start script.
example: Setting up any new Node project.

explain: module.exports shares something from a file; require loads it.
The newer import/export style. Turn it on with "type": "module".
Write a file, then read it back as text ("utf8").
appendFileSync adds to the end. existsSync checks if a file is there.
mkdirSync makes folders (recursive makes the parents too). readdirSync lists a folder.
renameSync renames or moves a file. unlinkSync deletes it.

syntax:
const path = require("path");
console.log(path.basename("/a/b/photo.jpg"), path.extname("photo.jpg"), path.dirname("/a/b/photo.jpg"));
explain: Get the file name, the extension, and the folder from a path.

syntax:
console.log(__dirname);
console.log(__filename);
explain: __dirname is the folder of this file, __filename is the file itself.
example: Finding files next to your script.

syntax: console.log(process.argv.slice(2));
explain: process.argv holds the words typed after "node file.js". slice(2) skips node and the file name.
example: A command-line tool: node app.js hello.

syntax:
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
console.log("port", port);
explain: process.env holds environment variables. || gives a default.
example: Secret keys and settings that change per computer.

explain: console.error prints to the error stream. process.exit(1) stops with a "failed" code.
example: Stopping when the user forgot something.

syntax:
const os = require("os");
console.log(os.platform(), os.homedir(), os.cpus().length);
explain: os tells you about the computer: system, home folder, number of CPU cores.
example: Scripts that work on Mac and Windows.

explain: A web server without any library. Every request runs the function.

syntax:
const url = new URL("https://example.com/search?q=cats&page=2");
console.log(url.hostname, url.searchParams.get("q"));
explain: URL splits a web address into parts.
on listens for an event, emit sends one.
example: Letting parts of an app talk to each other.

explain: await pauses an async function until the Promise is done.
Promise.all waits for many things at once.
example: Loading several files at the same time.

explain: With await, use try/catch for errors. ENOENT means "file not found".
Save data as a JSON file and load it back. null, 2 makes it neat.
example: A tiny database in a file.

explain: fetch is built into Node 18+. It downloads from a URL.
readline asks a question in the terminal and waits for an answer.

syntax:
const { execSync } = require("child_process");
console.log(execSync("echo hi from the shell").toString());
explain: execSync runs a terminal command and gives back what it printed.

syntax:
const buf = Buffer.from("hi");
console.log(buf, buf.toString("base64"));
explain: A Buffer is raw bytes. It can turn text into base64 and back.
Make unique ids and hashes.
example: Ids for new records; checking a file didn't change.

explain: A stream reads a file piece by piece, so huge files don't fill memory.
assert stops with an error if something is not what you expect.
Node has a built-in test runner.

syntax:
npm install express
npm install --save-dev nodemon
npm uninstall express
explain: install adds a package (saved in package.json). --save-dev is for tools you only need while building.

syntax:
npm run start
npx create-vite my-app
npm list
npm outdated
explain: npm run runs a script from package.json. npx runs a tool without installing it.
scripts in package.json are short names for commands. --watch restarts when files change.
:name in a route becomes req.params.name.
req.query holds the ?key=value parts. res.json sends JSON.
express.json() reads JSON sent to you into req.body. status sets the result code.
example: Saving data sent from a form.

syntax: app.use(express.static("public"));
explain: Serves every file in the public folder (HTML, CSS, images).
Middleware runs before your routes. next() passes to the next one.

syntax: app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).send("Not found"));
explain: A last app.use with no path catches anything nothing else answered.
setInterval repeats; clearInterval stops it.

syntax:
node app.js
node --watch app.js
node -e "console.log(1 + 1)"
explain: Run a file, run and restart on changes, or run one line.
